Section 20 ratifies all temporary regulations issued under Executive Order 7321 of March 21, 1936 and revokes those and all other annual leave regulations in so far as they are inconsistent with these regulations. These are one-time commands performed when the order was issued on 1938-03-21; section 21 makes the order effective as of January 1, 1938, which is the alternative effective date a reviewer should see. The ratification and revocation were exhausted by performance on issuance; a later supersession of the whole order is not their first end (see research/readiness/owner_rulings/2026-10-28-evidence-not-convenience.md).

Section 21 provides that the order is effective as of January 1, 1938 and, as of that date, supersedes Executive Order 7409 of July 9, 1936 on annual leave. The supersession of Executive Order 7409 was performed by issuing this order on 1938-03-21 with effect from 1938-01-01 (the alternative date); the command is exhausted by performance and the superseded order stays superseded whatever later happened to Executive Order 7845. The order-level supersession by Executive Order 8384 is therefore not this clause's first end.

Section 22 directs that the order be published in the Federal Register. The held Federal Register pages carry the issue date "Wednesday, March 23, 1938" in their running headers and the document line shows filing on March 22, 1938, so the command was performed by publication in the March 23, 1938 issue; it is exhausted by performance.

conflict_resolutions.FULL_AND_PARTIAL_EVIDENCE_CONFLICT: The Office of the Federal Register note on EO 7845 reads 'EO 8384, March 29, 1940 (in part)'. The text supports a whole supersession of EO 7845, effective as of March 2, 1940, and the note's 'in part' is read as the editorial reflection of the saving carve-out for sections 6 and 9, which is disclosed in the reasons for those two clauses.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 7845 of March 21, 1938 prescribes regulations on annual leave for civilian officers and employees of the United States, the District of Columbia and covered corporations under section 7 of the act of March 14, 1936 (49 Stat. 1161). The held text is the Federal Register print as machine-extracted from the official PDF (3 FR 715 to 717). The dossier inventory is corrected in four ways: an enacting-paragraph clause is added; section 9 and section 19(e) are each split at a page break so the Federal Register page header and table of contents are not carried inside a clause; section 19(e) is separated from section 19(f), which the machine segmentation merged because the held text prints (f) as "if)"; and Part headings are trimmed from the ends of sections 1(i) and 18. Sections 20 through 22 are retained. Executive Order 8384, signed 1940-03-29, states that it supersedes Executive Orders No. 7845, No. 7879 and No. 8226 and is effective as of March 2, 1940, so the continuing regulatory clauses end on 1940-03-02; its sections 6 and 9 are effective as of July 1, 1936 for leave adjustments, which is disclosed for sections 6 and 9. Section 20 (ratification and revocation of inconsistent regulations), section 21 (effective date and supersession of Executive Order 7409) and section 22 (publication) are one-time commands exhausted by performance, recorded with their performance dates rather than the later supersession. Section 6 was restated by Executive Order 7879 (signed 1938-05-09, effective as of January 1, 1938) and section 15 by Executive Order 8226 (signed 1939-08-24, effective as of June 30, 1939); both are later events recorded at their stated effective dates, with before-and-after text, not ends. Conflict on Executive Order 8384: the Office of the Federal Register note on this order reads 'EO 8384, March 29, 1940 (in part)', which the dossier flags as a whole-and-partial conflict. The held text of section 21 of Executive Order 8384 says 'This order shall supersede' Executive Orders No. 7845, No. 7879 and No. 8226 without limiting words, and carves out only the effective dates of its own sections 6 and 9; the supersession is read as whole. The dossier's chain also lists EO 7880 as a section 6 amendment; the held page for EO 7880 is the same Federal Register page (3 FR 1075) that carries EO 7879, and EO 7880 amends section 9 of EO 7846 (sick leave), not this order, so it is not a later event of this order.

The one-time commands in sections 20 to 22 are tied to their performance dates, shown in each clause. The dossier's EO 7880 edge comes from the shared Federal Register page and concerns the sick-leave order 7846, so it is not an end or amendment of this order.","independent_command_check":"Sections 20 and 21 contain one-time commands (ratify and revoke; supersede Executive Order 7409) that were performed when the order took effect and so ended by performance before the supersession; section 22 (publication) was performed on publication. Every other clause is part of the regulations that Executive Order 8384 supersedes.","savings_check":"Leave earned and used under EO 7845 before the supersession accrued; EO 8384 section 21 only caps adjusted leave credit at the statutory maximum and does not state a carry-forward, so none is asserted.","scope_check":"The corrected inventory covers the enacting paragraph and every numbered section and lettered subsection of the held text (sections 1 through 22), with sections 9 and 19(e) split at page breaks."}

savings.reason: Executive Order 8384 supersedes the order and re-prescribes the annual leave regime. Its section 21 proviso caps the total leave credited as a result of adjusting leave on the basis of the amended regulations at the amount authorized to be accumulated by law; it does not itself state that leave credits earned under EO 7845 are carried forward. Leave accrued and used under EO 7845 before the supersession is an accrued consequence of a performed regime, and no held source shows a loss of that leave, so the savings state records that the effects of the superseded regulations accrued before 1940-03-02 and the later order governs thereafter.
